Seneca sells packaged foods mainly to retailers and foodservice businesses, while Wendy’s serves diners and franchisees. Their products, buyer groups and business models differ.
labels.notes_matthew: Seneca makes canned and frozen vegetables and sells them to grocers and private label buyers. Almost all of their $1.7B is packaged food, nothing to do with running restaurants.

B&G sells packaged grocery foods rather than restaurant meals. Food-related products alone do not make it a peer.
labels.notes_matthew: B&G owns grocery brands like Green Giant and Crisco and sells through retailers and distributors. A packaged food company is not a restaurant comp.

Both serve dining customers, but Flanigan’s focuses on casual dining and liquor retail rather than burger-led quick service.
labels.notes_matthew: Flanigan's does run restaurants, but about 23% of its sales come from package liquor stores and the restaurants are full service bar and grills. It is also only 37 locations in South Florida on $205M, so I can't call it a direct comp.

labels.notes_matthew: SunOpta makes private label oat milk and fruit snacks for retailers and other food brands. It is a contract manufacturer, not a restaurant.

Tootsie Roll sells packaged confectionery through retailers. Candy sales have different customers and economics from restaurant service.
labels.notes_matthew: Tootsie Roll makes candy and sells it wholesale to retailers. Both are food in the loosest sense but the business is completely different.

Coca-Cola Consolidated bottles and distributes beverages to businesses. It does not compete as a restaurant operator or franchisor.
labels.notes_matthew: Coke Consolidated is a bottler. Restaurants like Wendy's are its customers, which makes it a supplier rather than a competitor.

Both compete for dining spending, but ONE Group focuses on full-service and experiential restaurants rather than value-oriented quick service.
labels.notes_matthew: The ONE Group is a real restaurant operator, but the brands are STK and Benihana with average checks over $100. Their 10-K doesn't even mention quick service chains as competitors, so I'd call this adjacent at best.

Both serve restaurant diners, but Texas Roadhouse focuses on casual table-service dining rather than quick-service burgers.
labels.notes_matthew: Texas Roadhouse is a mass market casual dining chain with 816 units, and its 10-K names quick service and fast casual chains as competitors. Different format from Wendy's but the same business selling meals to the same consumers.

Carter’s sells children’s clothing. Its products and purchasing needs differ from restaurant meals.

Hormel sells packaged foods to retail and foodservice buyers. It is a food manufacturer rather than a restaurant operator.
labels.notes_matthew: Hormel is packaged meat. About a third of its sales go to foodservice, which again makes it a supplier to restaurants rather than a peer.

Different industry; Different products; Different customer needs; Different business model

Church & Dwight sells household and personal-care products. These do not overlap with restaurant meals or franchise services.
labels.notes_matthew: Church & Dwight is Arm & Hammer and OxiClean. Household products, no food or restaurant business.

labels.notes_barbara:
Overlapping HR buyers; Partial product overlap; Different core offering

DHI’s recruitment tools overlap with HR buyers and hiring workflows. They do not replace Paylocity’s payroll and broader HCM platform.
labels.notes_matthew: DHI runs the Dice and ClearanceJobs job boards and sells posting packages to recruiters and staffing firms. Its competitors are LinkedIn and Indeed, not human resources software companies.

labels.notes_barbara:
Overlapping customers; Different business model; Different delivery model

Both serve small and midsize employers, but BBSI uses a PEO/co-employment model rather than HCM software. Scored 1 under the rubric’s customer-overlap rule.
labels.notes_matthew: BBSI is a PEO (professional employer organization), which is 94% of its revenue. It handles payroll, human resources and benefits for small businesses through co-employment, meaning it becomes the legal employer of record. So the customer is similar to Paylocity's but the product is a service, not software.

labels.notes_barbara:
Overlapping customer segment; Different products; Different functional buyers

RingCentral serves some of the same small and midsize business customers. Its communications products differ from payroll and HCM.
labels.notes_matthew: RingCentral sells cloud phone systems and contact center software to IT (information technology) departments. Its competitors are Zoom, Microsoft and Cisco. The only link to Paylocity is that both are cloud subscriptions.

labels.notes_barbara:
Same core products; Overlapping customers

Asure offers payroll, HR, tax and time-management software to small and midsize employers. Both the products and customer segment overlap.
labels.notes_matthew: Asure sells payroll, tax, human resources and time tracking software to small and mid-sized employers, and its 10-K literally names Paylocity as a main competitor. It's much smaller at $140M but it's the same business.

labels.notes_riya: different industry (health) but similar functionality
labels.notes_barbara:
Partial product overlap; Overlapping HR buyers; Different revenue model

HealthEquity overlaps in employer benefits administration. Its HSA custody and account-fee model differs from a full payroll/HCM platform.
labels.notes_matthew: HealthEquity sells HSAs (health savings accounts) and benefits administration to employer benefits teams, so it's the same human resources buyer. But most of its revenue comes from custodial fees and card interchange fees, not software, so it's adjacent rather than direct.

labels.notes_barbara:
Different products; Different customers; Different core workflows

SS&C focuses on investment and financial-services operations. Its specialist institutional workflows differ from employer payroll and HR.
labels.notes_matthew: SS&C does fund administration and software for asset managers and banks. There is no payroll or human resources product here.

labels.notes_barbara:
Partial product/customer overlap; Broader business mix

QuickBooks payroll overlaps with small-business payroll needs. Intuit’s broader tax, accounting and consumer businesses make the whole company adjacent.
labels.notes_matthew: Intuit has QuickBooks Payroll, which does overlap with Paylocity, but it mostly serves very small businesses and about 40% of Intuit's revenue is TurboTax and Credit Karma. Partial overlap at best.

labels.notes_barbara:
Partial product overlap; Different customer focus; Different business model; Outdated payroll description

Alight overlaps in employer benefits administration, particularly for larger employers. Its former payroll outsourcing business was sold, limiting the payroll match.
labels.notes_matthew: Alight does benefits administration outsourcing for large employers, so same human resources buyer. But it sold its payroll business in 2024 and its named competitors are ADP and HealthEquity, not the mid-market HCM (human capital management, meaning payroll and human resources software) vendors.

labels.notes_barbara:
Same core products; Overlapping customers; Broader business mix

ADP offers payroll and HCM to small and midsize employers as well as large enterprises. Its overlapping products and customers make it a direct competitor.
labels.notes_matthew: ADP's Workforce Now product serves around 90,000 mid-sized employers with payroll and HCM (human capital management) software, which is exactly Paylocity's market. Paylocity's own 10-K names ADP as a competitor. Way bigger company but the same business.

labels.notes_barbara:
Partial HR product overlap; Overlapping HR buyers; Different core offering

Upland FileBound supports hiring, onboarding and employee-document workflows, creating overlap with Paylocity’s HR tools. Its broader portfolio does not provide the same core payroll/HCM offering, so it is adjacent.
labels.notes_matthew: Upland is a collection of document and marketing workflow tools sold to IT (information technology) and marketing teams. No payroll or human resources product.

labels.notes_barbara:
Different products; Different functional buyers; Different customer focus

Sprinklr serves enterprise marketing and customer-service teams. Its products and functional buyers differ from HR/payroll.
labels.notes_matthew: Sprinklr is customer experience software for marketing teams at big enterprises. No human resources angle.

labels.notes_barbara:
Overlapping customer segment; Different products; Different business mix

Thryv serves small businesses with marketing and business-management tools. Customer overlap supports adjacency, but payroll/HCM is not its core offering.
labels.notes_matthew: Thryv sells marketing and CRM (customer relationship management) software to small business owners and still gets about 40% of its revenue from Yellow Pages ads. No payroll or human resources product.

labels.notes_riya: donnelley deals wtih compliance software
labels.notes_barbara:
Different products; Different functional buyers; Different regulatory workflows

DFIN serves securities-reporting and capital-markets compliance needs. Its buyers and workflows differ from employer payroll and HR.
labels.notes_matthew: Donnelley Financial does SEC filing and compliance software for public companies. The buyer is legal and finance, not human resources.

labels.notes_barbara:
Different core products; Different functional buyers; Limited knowledge-management overlap

eGain primarily supports customer-service knowledge and customer interactions, while Paylocity focuses on payroll and employee management. Shared AI or knowledge features do not establish a direct payroll/HCM match.
labels.notes_matthew: eGain is customer service knowledge software for contact centers at banks and telecoms. It's also under $100M in revenue. No human resources overlap.

labels.notes_barbara:
Same core products; Overlapping customers

Paycom provides cloud payroll and employee-lifecycle HCM to employers. Both its product suite and customer market overlap with Paylocity.
labels.notes_matthew: Paycom is cloud payroll and HCM (human capital management) software for employers from 50 to 10,000 employees, and its 10-K names Paylocity as a competitor. This is the closest comp in the whole pool.

labels.notes_riya: progress software corp doesn't really help businesses automate and manage the entire employee lifecycle from a single system
labels.notes_barbara:
Different products; Different functional buyers

Progress sells application-development and IT tools. Its developer and IT buyers differ from HR/payroll users.
labels.notes_matthew: Progress sells developer tools and IT (information technology) infrastructure software, half of it through OEMs (original equipment manufacturers who bundle it into their own products). No human resources or payroll product.
